Elementary Matrices and LU Factorization – Linear Algebra: Lecture Notes

Previously, we saw how the linear system [latex]A\vec{x}=\vec b[/latex] can be solved by using Gaussian elimination. In this section we show how, in certain cases, an [latex]m \times n[/latex] matrix [latex]A[/latex] can be written as [latex]A=LU[/latex], where [latex]L[/latex] is a lower triangular matrix and [latex]U[/latex] is an upper triangular matrix. We call this an [latex]LU[/latex] factorization of [latex]A[/latex].

An [latex]LU[/latex] factorization of the matrix [latex]\left[ \begin{array}{rr} -3 & -2\\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right][/latex] is given by

[latex]\left[ \begin{array}{rr} -3 & -2\\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right]= \left[ \begin{array}{rr} -1 & 0\\ 1 & 2 \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{rr} 3 & 2\\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right][/latex]

An elementary matrix is any matrix that can be obtained from the identity matrix by performing a single elementary row operation.

Let [latex]A[/latex] be an [latex]m\times n[/latex] matrix and [latex]E[/latex] the elementary matrix obtained from the [latex]m\times m[/latex] identity matrix [latex]I[/latex] by a single row operation [latex]\mathcal R[/latex]. Denote [latex]\mathcal R(A)[/latex] the result of performing the row operation on [latex]A[/latex]. Then [latex]\mathcal R(A)=EA[/latex].

Remark 1.7.4

By repeated application of the above theorem, a sequence of row operations can be performed on a matrix [latex]A[/latex] by successively multiplying [latex]A[/latex] by the corresponding elementary matrices. Specifically, let [latex]E_i[/latex] be the elementary matrix corresponding to the row operation [latex]\mathcal R_i[/latex] with [latex]1 \leq i \leq k[/latex]. Then

[latex]\mathcal R_k \cdots \mathcal R_2(\mathcal R_1(A))=E_k \cdots E_2E_1A.[/latex]

Let [latex]A[/latex] be the matrix

[latex]A= \left[ \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 2 & -1\\ 3 & 5 & 0\\ -1 & 1 & 1 \end{array} \right][/latex]

Use elementary matrices to perform the row operations

[latex]\mathcal R_1: - 3R_1 + R_2 \to R_2, \mathcal R_2: R_1 + R_3 \to R_3[/latex] and [latex]\mathcal R_3: 3R_2 + R_3 \to R_3[/latex].

The elementary matrices corresponding to these row operations are given by

Remark 1.7.6

Note that the matrix on the right-hand side above is equal to the result of performing the row operations on [latex]A[/latex] in the order given. Namely,

Recall that an [latex]m\times n[/latex] matrix [latex]A[/latex] is row equivalent to an [latex]m\times n[/latex] matrix [latex]B[/latex] if [latex]B[/latex] can be obtained by a finite sequence of row operations. The next theorem gives a restatement of this fact in terms of elementary matrices.
